analysis.one_liner: Bars states from taxing out-of-state companies' income unless those companies have a physical presence in the state.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 18-7 in June 2015, but it never received a vote by the full House and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1959, federal law has stopped states from collecting income taxes from out-of-state companies that do nothing more in a state than solicit sales. This bill would expand that shield: it would cover services and intangible property, not just goods, extend it to other business taxes beyond income taxes, and write a hard rule that a state can tax a company only if the company has employees, property, or a dedicated agent physically in the state. Companies selling into a state from outside it — including online sellers — would largely stop owing state business taxes there.
analysis.who_benefits: Multistate corporations, especially online retailers, software and services companies, and other businesses that sell into many states without a physical footprint there. They would owe far less in state business taxes, and independent contractors or affiliates working for them in a state would no longer create a taxable presence. State governments lose the offsetting gain: less revenue means either cut services or higher taxes on in-state businesses and residents.

how_it_helps.text: Expands the 1959 federal protection (Public Law 86-272) so it covers not just sales of physical goods but also services, intangible property, and other transactions fulfilled from outside a state [S2][S3].
Extends the protection beyond income taxes to other business activity taxes, such as gross-receipts and franchise-style taxes, starting with tax periods beginning January 1, 2016 [S3].

Prohibits a state from imposing these taxes unless the company has a physical presence there — an employee physically in the state, owned or leased property, or an exclusive in-state agent — with a de minimis exception for presence under 15 days a year [S2][S3].
Provides that activity by independent contractors — sales, solicitation, furnishing information — does not by itself create a taxable presence for the company they work for [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments lose revenue they currently collect from out-of-state companies doing business with their residents. That shortfall gets made up by cutting services, raising taxes on in-state businesses and residents, or both. In-state businesses that pay state taxes would also compete against out-of-state rivals selling into the same market tax-free.

drawbacks.text: States would lose tax revenue from companies earning money from their residents; because states must balance their budgets, that gap tends to come back to residents as service cuts or higher taxes [S2].
The physical-presence rule gives out-of-state sellers a structural advantage over local businesses, which must pay state taxes on the same sales into the same market [S3].

A good-faith supporter's acknowledged trade-off: the bill makes state tax rules simpler and more predictable for companies operating nationwide, but it settles that simplicity on the side of taxing local activity rather than remote sales [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplicity and certainty the bill offers national businesses is real, but the design pushes the cost onto state budgets and onto local businesses competing against untaxed remote sellers. It is a broad tax shelter for companies with no physical footprint in the states where they earn sales, and the revenue loss would be made up by the people and businesses that remain taxable there.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee with an 18-7 vote to send it to the floor, but no one ever scheduled it for a full House vote, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Chabot introduced the bill on June 1, 2015, joined by Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S3][S4].
It had one cosponsor, a Democrat [S4].

The bill got an unusually fast committee process: a subcommittee hearing the day after referral, the subcommittee discharged it on June 16, and the full committee marked it up and ordered it reported by a vote of 18-7 on June 17, 2015 [S5].
No further action was taken for the rest of the Congress; the bill was never reported to the floor or voted on by the full House [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments kept their current authority to tax out-of-state companies doing business with their residents, and in-state businesses avoided a new competitive disadvantage against remote sellers. The multistate companies the bill was written for did not get the expanded federal tax shield.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with one Democratic cosponsor, and the committee approved it 18-7, but the record does not give a party breakdown of that vote or of any floor opposition.

industries.industry: Multistate and online sellers (retail, software, and services)
industries.note: The bill would exempt companies without a physical presence from state business taxes on sales made into a state, letting them earn revenue from a state's residents without contributing to its budget. Their gain is a cost borne by state services and in-state taxpayers.

States would lose tax revenue from out-of-state companies and could no longer extend tax reach through contractors, affiliates, or economic activity alone. Because states must balance budgets, the loss tends to fall back on residents and in-state businesses.

Local businesses would pay state business taxes as before while competing against out-of-state rivals selling into the same market tax-free. The bill does not raise their taxes, but it widens the competitive gap.

industries.industry: Independent contractors and affiliates of remote sellers
industries.note: Their activities in a state could no longer create a taxable presence for the companies they represent, expanding the shelter for the firms that use them.
